text.p: Violence against Jews waned worldwide last year but hate groups are increasingly turning to the Internet to spread anti-Semitism, said a report released in Israel on Sunday.

"Hate groups which are quite marginalised in society and found it difficult to disseminate anti-Semitism now have the potential to reach hundreds of thousands, if not millions, on their websites," said Harry Wall of the Anti-Defamation League (ADL).
The ADL, along with the World Jewish Congress, helped produce the annual "Anti-Semitism Worldwide" report by Tel Aviv University.
The survey found that major attacks -- defined as shootings, firebombs and arson -- against Jews declined worldwide from 41 in 1995 to 32 last year.

"Not all the reasons for this decline are discernible...yet one might assume that in part it is the result of more stringent enforcement of existing and new anti-racist and anti-terrorist laws," the report said.
But Wall pointed to what he called "a growing concern over dissemination of anti-Semitic propaganda", particularly via the Internet and e-mail.
The report listed 39 World Wide Web sites it considered anti-Semitic and said many were placed on free or individual homepages provided by companies that link computer users to the Internet.

Wall said the U.S.-based ADL faced a dilemma in dealing with anti-Semitism on the Internet because the ADL "doesn't believe in censorship". But he said the ADL does warn Internet providers that U.S. laws ban incitement to racism.

The report pointed to a 17 percent decline since 1994 in anti-Semitic incidents, including acts against property and individuals, in the United States. It noted a decline in major attacks against Jews in Western Europe from 15 to nine.

"But on the other hand, in 1996, the extreme right camp continued to enhance its political position in Western Europe," it said, mentioning Joerg Haider's Freedom Party in Austria and Jean-Marie Le Pen's National Front in France.

In Switzerland, in the spotlight over Jewish claims for bank deposits made before World War Two by Jews later killed in the Nazi Holocaust, anti-Semitic propaganda was on the rise last year, the report said.

"Jewish organisations and individuals have received hundreds of anti-Semitic letters daily, compared to approximately two letters per month before the revelations," it said. "In addition, Swiss newspapers publish pages of anti-Semitic letters to the editor"
Two of Israel's Arab peace partners, Egypt and Jordan, were criticised for what the report said were expressions of anti-Semitism, especially in the Egyptian press.

"It seemed that the most virulent attacks emanated from these countries, either due to frustration with the peace process or to an attempt by (Islamic) fundamentalists to bring it to an end in a rearguard action," the survey said.
But one of the report's editors, Dina Porat, told the news conference a clear line could not always be drawn between where "anti-Israeli and anti-Zionist (expression) ends and anti-Semitism begins".
